issue.title: TS SDK: name a task's inputs, and take its id from the handler

repository.name: airflow
repository.description: Apache Airflow - A platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows

issue.body:
- **Diff for early review**: https://github.com/apache/airflow/compare/main...jason810496:airflow:feature/ts-sdk/default-task-id-at-pack-time
- **next**: #73438
- #73436 is merged, so this one applies to `main` on its own.
- Part of the native TypeScript Dag stack, #73435 to #73446, to be merged in order.

## Why

Every argument reaches the serialized Dag by name, and a positional parameter list has none unless the SDK reads them out of the handler's source. A handler that takes one object of named arguments is what a TypeScript library takes anyway, and it settles both ends: the call site carries the names, and the handler's own name is still the task id.

```ts
const transform = dag.task(
  "transform",
  async ({ rows, region }: { rows: number; region: string }) => rows * 2,
);

transform({ rows: extracted, region: "us" });
```

## How

- A call records its own keys, so nothing reads a function's parameter list and no argument is ever labelled `arg0`. `TaskOptions.argBindings` is gone with it.
- A handler that declares more than one parameter, or a call given more than one argument, is an error, so a positional call from plain JavaScript fails instead of losing a value.
- `dag.task(handler)` takes its id from `handler.name`, and `TaskSpec.taskId` sets one for an anonymous handler. Giving the id twice is an error rather than a silent winner.
- `airflow-ts-pack` passes esbuild's `keepNames`, so the id survives minification.

`ts-sdk/adr/0002` records the positional handler as tried and dropped. An earlier revision of this PR read the names at pack time with an esbuild `onLoad` hook and TypeScript's parser; it needed a parser in the packer and could not see a handler declared in another module.

issue.title: Validate the ids of a serialized language-SDK Dag

repository.name: airflow
repository.description: Apache Airflow - A platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows

issue.body:
A Dag that a language SDK serializes reaches Airflow as serialized-Dag JSON, so the id checks in the Task SDK's constructors never run on it. A TypeScript, Go or Java Dag with a dag id, task id or task group id that is too long or made of other characters is stored as is; on Postgres the 250-character columns turn that into a database error instead of an import error. The SDKs' pack-time warnings say the server will reject such ids, and it did not.

`validate_serialized_dag` now applies the Task SDK's rules: 250 characters and `[\w.-]` for the dag id and task ids, 200 characters and `[\w-]` for each task group's own id, raising `DeserializationError`, which the Dag processor records as an import error against the file. Only Dags from language SDKs pass through this function, so Python Dags are untouched, and the `..` rule stays where the Task SDK has it, on connection and run ids. Compared with #73923, the task group ids come from the deserialized task group tree rather than a walk over the raw children, and the rules match the Task SDK rather than core's `validate_key`, so ids with `..` that Python Dags carry today keep loading.

Tested with a packed TypeScript bundle declaring five Dags (valid, task id of 260 characters, task id `has space!`, dag id of 260 characters, dag id with spaces) parsed by `airflow dag-processor`: before, all five were stored; after, the valid one loads and the file gets one import error naming each of the other four. Unit tests cover each id kind, too long and with other characters, plus the ids the SDK accepts.

closes: #73800
related: #73923

I opened #75569 for this: the dag, task and task group ids are checked in `validate_serialized_dag` with the Task SDK's own rules, so a bad id from a language-SDK bundle becomes an import error on the file. The `..` rule is left as the Task SDK has it, which is where #73923 ran into trouble.

Reviews or comments appreciated, thanks!
